one_liner: Pure-Python, SQLite-backed persistent cache that runs in-process and beats localhost Memcached/Redis on read latency, not writes.
what_it_does: DiskCache keeps key/value pairs in a directory on local disk, as one SQLite database plus value files. Threads and processes on the same machine can share it safely, so you get a persistent, size-bounded cache without running a server. `Cache` offers a dict-like mapping plus memcached-style get/set/add/incr/decr/delete/touch with expiry and tags. `FanoutCache` shards it, `DjangoCache` plugs into Django's cache framework, and `Deque`/`Index` and recipes (memoize_stampede, Lock, throttle) build on top. It does not speak the Memcached or Redis wire protocol, so callers must use the Python API.
how_it_is_fast: Gets skip the network round trip: the cache is an embedded SQLite database queried in-process, while the Memcached and Redis baselines go through a localhost socket. SQLite runs in write-ahead-log (WAL) mode so reads and writes don't block each other, with a 64 MB mmap and an 8,192-page page cache. Values under 32 KB are stored inline and larger ones in separate files, and SQLite triggers keep count and size so nothing needs a scan. Under the default least-recently-stored eviction policy a get is one indexed SELECT with no transaction and no write. FanoutCache hashes keys (adler32) across N SQLite files, so concurrent writers compete for N write locks instead of one.
when_to_use: A Python app on a single host (web workers, CLI tools, data pipelines) that needs a cache shared between its processes and kept across restarts, without running Memcached or Redis.
Read-dominated traffic (around 90% gets) with small keys and values, where in-process gets beat a localhost Memcached round trip (median 12.2 us vs 26.0 us in the author's benchmark).
Caches larger than RAM: gigabytes on local disk, with large values written to files and readable as file handles (`read=True`).
Memoizing expensive function results across runs (`memoize`, `memoize_stampede` for cache-stampede protection).
Django sites that want a replacement for the built-in file-based cache, via `DjangoCache`.
when_not_to_use: Write-heavy traffic, or many writers on one unsharded `Cache`: writers take turns on SQLite's write lock. With 8 processes, set P99 was 21.3 ms and the max 1.85 s, against a 312 us max for Memcached. Single-process sets are also about 2.5x slower than Memcached (68.9 us vs 27.9 us median).
Caches shared between machines: there is no network interface, and SQLite is not recommended on NFS. The docs also report poor performance on PythonAnywhere and problems in Parallels shared folders.

Cache directories writable by less-trusted code: the default Disk unpickles values on read. CVE-2025-69872 / GHSA-w8v5-vhqr-4h9v (medium) covers all versions up to 5.6.3 with no patched release. Use JSONDisk or lock down the directory.
LRU/LFU eviction or statistics: these turn every get into a write transaction, which gives up the fast read path the benchmark measured. The benchmark ran the default least-recently-stored policy.

asyncio code (no native async; wrap calls in a thread executor), or many threads under a tight memory budget: each thread opens its own SQLite connection and mmap. In issue #293, 10 threads peaked at 2.15 GB RSS against 0.13 GB for one thread.

integration.dependencies: none (uses only the standard-library sqlite3 module)
integration.min_toolchain: Python 3 (setup.py python_requires '>=3'); CI tests CPython 3.8-3.11; current release 5.6.3
integration.platforms: any platform with Python's sqlite3 on a local filesystem; CI runs on Linux, macOS and Windows; not NFS
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe and process-safe: one SQLite connection per thread (threading.local), reopened after fork. Readers don't block writers, but writers block other writers on the same shard.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the get/set/add/incr/delete/touch-with-expiry API resembles a memcached client and DjangoCache swaps into Django's cache settings, but there is no Memcached/Redis protocol and no cross-host sharing, so client code must change

gotchas: FanoutCache's default timeout is 10 ms, and set/delete swallow the Timeout and return False, so writes can fail silently (39 of 71,530 sets were dropped in the 8-process benchmark). A plain `Cache` raises Timeout instead, with a 60 s default.

Keys are matched by their serialized bytes, not by __hash__/__eq__. Pickled container keys such as tuples can serialize differently when equal (issue #54), and 1 and 1.0 count as the same key. Use JSONDisk for consistent keys.

In FanoutCache, size_limit (default 1 GB) is split evenly across shards, and an item larger than one shard's share is culled immediately. Culling is lazy (at most cull_limit=10 keys per write), so the cache can briefly exceed its limit.

Open bug #325: on macOS, forking after opening two `Cache` objects on the same directory gives sqlite3 'disk I/O error'. A full disk raises sqlite3.OperationalError on any write, but reads keep working.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick DiskCache over server caches like Pogocache, Valkey or Dragonfly when the cache lives on one machine inside a Python app and you want persistence and no server to run. Those siblings win when the cache must be shared across hosts or has to absorb heavy concurrent writes.
verified_claims_summary: The author's tests/benchmark_core.py runs 100k ops per process (90% get, 9% set, 1% delete) over only 100 keys with values of a few hundred bytes, so the whole working set stays hot in SQLite's page cache. It pits DiskCache in-process against pylibmc and redis-py talking to default-configured localhost servers. Single-process median get was 12.2 us vs 26.0 us (Memcached) and 44.1 us (Redis), and median set was 68.9 us vs 27.9 us. With 8 processes, only FanoutCache(8 shards) beat Memcached overall (59.0 s vs 68.8 s total); plain Cache took 157.9 s. The page gives no CPU, OS, Python, SQLite, Memcached or Redis versions, its tables date from 2017, and the committed tests/timings_core_p1.txt comes from a different run (19.1 us get median).
status_note: Stale: last commit 2024-03-03 and last release 5.6.3 (2023-08-31), with 85 open issues. In July 2026 the maintainer declined to commit to a fix or timeline for the pickle CVE. It is Apache-2.0, pure Python and dependency-free, so it is easy to vendor or fork.
